subject: Follow-up: Pseudonymization vs Masking for Request/Response Logs (post-call)
messages:
From: Irene Choi <irene.choi@redwood.ai>
To: Dr. Priya Shah <priya.shah@acme-health.com>, Jake Turner <jake.turner@acme-health.com>
Cc: Aditya Rao <aditya_rao@redwood.ai>, Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.ai>
Date: 2027-04-02T15:10:00-07:00
Subject: Follow-up: Pseudonymization vs Masking for Request/Response Logs (post-call)

Thanks again for the call earlier today — really appreciate the clear breakdown of Acme's audit requirements. I wanted to capture the options we walked through and the immediate asks so your security and engineering teams have something concrete to review.

Recap of the options we discussed (high level):
- Full redaction: drop PII fields from logs entirely (safe for privacy, harder for debugging)
- Deterministic pseudonymization: replace identifiers with stable tokens (e.g., HMAC(key, user_id)) so traces across systems correlate but original value isn't stored in logs
- Reversible tokenization: encrypt or token-store mapping (needed if you must re-identify records for support/legal)
- Field-level masking: truncate or mask characters (useful for emails/SSNs)

Specific telemetry we covered: request/response bodies, HTTP headers (common sensitive fields: Authorization, Cookie, x-session-id, x-trace-id), and URL query params. You flagged x-trace-id: you want correlation across microservices but without exposing the raw user identifier that sometimes gets injected into trace metadata.

Questions we promised to get you answers to:
1) Can you confirm the minimum required log retention windows for audit vs. support? (you mentioned 90 days for audits, 30 days for support in the call)
2) Is reversible re-identification permitted under any conditions (e.g., legal request with approved SSO) or is irreversible pseudonymization required?
3) Do you have a preferred key management approach for deterministic tokens (KMS/HSM managed by Acme vs. Redwood-managed KMS)?

Proposed near-term approach (recommended):
- Implement deterministic HMAC-based pseudonymization for user identifiers in request logs (configurable per-field). This gives correlation across components without storing raw IDs.
- Mask headers with known secrets (Authorization/Cookie) and keep a short hashed fingerprint for dedupe.
- Store an auditable mapping only if reversible tokenization is explicitly approved by Acme security; otherwise keep a single-way HMAC.

Attached: redaction-options-summary.pdf (one-page table comparing tradeoffs) and the data-flow diagram you shared with a few annotation suggestions (acme-data-flow-diagram.png).

Action items (Irene / Redwood):
- Provide a written matrix of tradeoffs and example log lines for your security team to review (deliverable: Monday 2027-04-05)
- Draft config snippets for our runtime to show how pseudonymization would be toggled (deliverable: next week)

Can we schedule a 30-min follow-up with your security architect the week of Apr 12 to agree on the final approach and KMS decisions?

Best,
Irene Choi
Senior Solutions Engineer
Redwood Inference

Attachments referenced: redaction-options-summary.pdf (1 page), acme-data-flow-diagram.png (PNG)

Subject: Re: Follow-up: Pseudonymization vs Masking for Request/Response Logs (post-call)

Thanks, Irene — this is helpful. A few clarifications from our side after syncing with InfoSec: 

- Retention: for regulatory audit we need 365 days of immutable audit logs for certain endpoints (billing and clinical workflows). For general telemetry, 90 days is fine.
- Re-identification: reversible mappings are allowed but only if the key is stored in our HSM and re-identification requests go through a formal approval workflow. We prefer irreversible pseudonymization for day-to-day telemetry.
- Trace IDs: we need correlation for incident response. Your deterministic HMAC approach sounds promising — can you give an example of the token format (length, charset), and whether the HMAC salt can be rotated without breaking correlation for existing traces?

Also attached is a sample schema of the headers we'd like to protect. We'll upload a redacted sample log file to the shared drive tonight.

Can we do Apr 13, 10am PT for the follow-up? Jake will join from infra.

—Priya
Chief Security Officer
Acme Health

Attachments referenced: acme-redacted-log-sample.log (will upload to drive)

From: Aditya Rao <aditya_rao@redwood.ai>
To: Dr. Priya Shah <priya.shah@acme-health.com>, Irene Choi <irene.choi@redwood.ai>
Cc: Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.ai>
Date: 2027-04-04T11:47:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Follow-up: Pseudonymization vs Masking for Request/Response Logs (post-call)

Hi Priya, thanks for the details — short answers below, we will include code snippets in the matrix on Monday.

- Example token: redwood uses a base62 stable token derived from HMAC-SHA256; e.g., rwd_1a7bCq9Z. Length and prefix are configurable; we can produce tokens between 8–24 chars.
- Salt rotation: deterministic HMAC requires the same key to preserve cross-time correlation. Options:
  * Keep one active HMAC key for correlation; rotate by creating a new key and backfilling/re-hashing historical data if you need correlation across the rotation window (expensive).
  * Maintain a key-rotation table where old keys are retained for verification for a defined window (we can store key metadata in your HSM).
- Reversible tokenization: if you choose reversible, we recommend storing the mapping in a customer-controlled vault (your HSM or a token DB under Acme's control). Redwood can integrate with customer KMS for encryption at rest.

We will also include a recommendation for storing only hashed fingerprints of Authorization/Cookie headers (HMAC truncated to 8 bytes) for dedupe/incident grouping without exposing secrets.

Confirming Apr 13, 10am PT for the follow-up with Jake. We'll send a calendar invite.

Thanks,
Aditya Rao
Solutions Lead, Sales Engineering
Redwood Inference

Attachment: none (Irene will attach the matrix)

Subject: Re: Follow-up: Pseudonymization vs Masking for Request/Response Logs (post-call)

Quick note from infra: thanks for the options. Two infra constraints to factor in before the meeting:
- We need any HMAC/tokenization code to run inline in the request pipeline (latency budget < 8ms per request). Please include a micro-benchmark for our expected QPS in the matrix.
- For 365-day immutable audit logs, we require write-once storage (WORM) or an append-only object store. Can Redwood push to our S3 with object lock or integrate with our SIEM instead?

I'll bring an artifact of our current pipeline (kinesis -> processor -> s3) to the Apr 13 call.

—Jake
Infra Lead
Acme Health
